sec.t:
आम कहानी कुछ यूँ है। 1971 में सोवियत इंजीनियर रेगिस्तान में तेल और गैस की तलाश में खुदाई कर रहे थे। उनकी खुदाई की मशीन ज़मीन के नीचे की एक खोखली जगह के ठीक ऊपर थी। ज़मीन धँस गई, और मशीन एक गड्ढे में जा गिरी।

गैस निकलने लगी। अकेली मीथेन ज़हरीली नहीं होती, पर गैस के भंडारों में अक्सर दूसरी नुकसानदेह गैसें भी होती हैं, और उनका एक बादल लोगों और जानवरों का दम घोंट सकता है। तो कहानी कहती है कि इंजीनियरों ने इसमें आग लगाकर गैस को जल जाने देने का फ़ैसला किया। उन्हें उम्मीद थी कि आग कुछ हफ़्तों में [[@fire-burns|जलकर]] बुझ जाएगी।

ऐसा नहीं हुआ। नीचे का गैस भंडार बहुत बड़ा है, और वह लपटों को खिलाता रहा।

तुर्कमेनिस्तान के कुछ भूवैज्ञानिक यह कहानी अलग ढंग से सुनाते हैं। वे कहते हैं कि गड्ढा 1960 के दशक में बना था और इसमें आग 1980 के दशक में जाकर लगी। पुराने रिकॉर्ड ग़ायब हैं, इसलिए कोई पक्के तौर पर नहीं कह सकता।

sec.h: तो इसे बुझा क्यों नहीं देते?
sec.t:
तुर्कमेनिस्तान के पास दुनिया के कुछ सबसे बड़े प्राकृतिक गैस भंडार हैं। यह वह ईंधन है जो [[@oil-coal|कोयले और तेल]] की तरह ही प्राचीन जीवों से बना। आग उस गैस को बर्बाद करती है जिसे बेचा जा सकता था। 2022 में देश के नेता ने अधिकारियों को आदेश दिया कि आग ख़त्म करने का कोई रास्ता खोजें।

पर लपटों को बस दबा देने से एक अलग मुसीबत खड़ी हो जाती। तब बिना जली मीथेन हवा में रिसने लगती। कुछ दशकों के हिसाब से मीथेन कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड से कहीं ज़्यादा गर्मी रोकती है, यानी यह एक ताकतवर [[greenhouse-gas|ग्रीनहाउस गैस]] है, और [[@climate-change|जलवायु परिवर्तन]] के लिए बड़ी चिंता है।

इसके बजाय इंजीनियरों ने पास में कुएँ खोदे, ताकि गैस गड्ढे तक पहुँचने से पहले ही खींच ली जाए। 2025 में अधिकारियों ने कहा कि आग सिकुड़कर पहले के लगभग एक-तिहाई आकार की रह गई है। गर्मी की नापों के एक विश्लेषण में पाया गया कि तीन सालों में आग की गर्मी तीन-चौथाई से भी ज़्यादा घट गई, हालाँकि 2025 के आख़िर में भी लपटों के छोटे-छोटे हिस्से जल रहे थे।

नरक का दरवाज़ा सालों से जलती अकेली आग नहीं है। झारखंड के झरिया में ज़मीन के नीचे कोयले की परतें लगभग 1916 से जल रही हैं। अमेरिका में पेनसिल्वेनिया के सेंट्रेलिया क़स्बे के नीचे कोयले की आग 1962 से सुलग रही है, और लगभग सभी लोग वहाँ से चले गए।

प्राकृतिक गैस की कुछ आगें इससे कहीं पुरानी हैं। तुर्की में एक पहाड़ी पर चट्टानों से निकलती किमेरा नाम की लपटें प्राचीन काल से टिमटिमा रही हैं। और सबसे अजीब बात? भारत की भी अपनी अखंड ज्योतियाँ हैं, जो [[@himachal|हिमाचल प्रदेश]] के ज्वालामुखी मंदिर में चट्टान से निकलती हैं और पवित्र मानी जाती हैं।

text: We have seasons because Earth is tilted. Its [[axis|axis]], the imaginary line it spins around, leans over by about 23.4°. As Earth travels around the Sun over a year, the axis keeps pointing the same way in space.

So for part of the year, the northern half of Earth leans towards the Sun. Sunlight there is more direct, days are longer, and it is summer. Six months later, the northern half leans away. Sunlight is slanted, days are shorter, and it is winter. The southern half has the opposite seasons.

sec.t:
Many people think summer comes when Earth is closest to the Sun. But Earth's [[orbit|orbit]] is almost a perfect circle, and Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of winter in India and the United States.

The tilt matters far more than the small change in distance. And if distance were the cause, the whole planet would have summer at the same time. Instead, when it's winter in Chicago, it's summer in Sydney.

When the Sun is high in the sky, its light hits the ground straight on, concentrating its energy on a small area. When the Sun is low, the same amount of light is spread over a larger area, so each patch of ground is warmed less. Slanted sunlight also passes through more air, which absorbs and scatters some of it.

Long days add to the effect. In summer, the Sun is up for more hours, so the ground has more time to warm. In winter, long nights give it more time to cool.

India sits close to the tropics. The Tropic of Cancer, the line where the Sun is directly overhead at noon on the June solstice, passes through [[@india-states-tour|eight Indian states]], from Gujarat to Mizoram. Near the tropics, temperatures change less between summer and winter than in places farther north.

So in much of India, the seasons people notice most are about rain. Many Indian [[@calendars|calendars]] traditionally divide the year into six seasons, or ritus, including Vasant (spring), Grishma (summer) and Varsha (the rains). The [[@monsoon|monsoon]] shapes life in India as much as heat and cold do.

Near the poles, the tilt makes seasons extreme. In Utqiagvik, the [[@extreme-northernmost-town|northernmost town]] in [[@alaska|Alaska]], the Sun doesn't set for about 80 days in summer. In winter, it doesn't rise for about two months.

At the South Pole, the Sun rises once a year, around the September [[equinox|equinox]], and sets once, around the March equinox. That's six months of daylight followed by six months of night. Scientists who spend winter at research stations in Antarctica don't see the Sun for months.

The longest day is around 21 June, but in Delhi the hottest days come in May and June, before the [[monsoon|monsoon]] rains cool things down. In much of the USA, the hottest weeks are usually in July. The land and sea take time to warm up, like a pot on a stove, so the hottest days often come a few weeks after the strongest sunshine.

text: Bamboo grows fast because it doesn't have to build much that is new. When a bamboo shoot pushes out of the ground, it is already as wide as it will ever be. Packed inside are all its sections, separated by rings called nodes, like the parts of a folded telescope.

Instead of making lots of new cells, the shoot stretches the ones it already has. Every section grows longer at the same time, so the whole stem shoots upwards. Some kinds of bamboo can grow close to a metre in a single day.
The energy for this sprint comes from food stored in a huge underground network of stems, called [[rhizome|rhizomes]], which link many stems together.

sec.h: A season to grow, years to harden
sec.t:
A bamboo stem reaches its full height in just a few months. After that it never grows taller. Over the next few years, its walls fill with tough fibres and silica, the same stuff as sand, and it becomes hard and strong.

Each year, new shoots come up from the rhizomes, so a bamboo clump keeps getting bigger. People in many parts of India and East Asia harvest the young shoots before they toughen and cook them as vegetables or pickles.

Most plants flower every year. Some bamboos wait for decades. One kind that grows across Mizoram and other parts of the northeast flowers roughly every 48 years. When it does, every plant of that kind flowers at almost the same time, across huge areas, and then dies.

The bamboo seeds are a feast for rats. Rat numbers explode, and when the seeds run out, the rats move into fields and eat the crops. In Mizoram this is called *mautam*. It brought terrible [[famine|famine]] in 1959. When it came again around 2006 to 2008, the government and villagers were better prepared.

How the plants keep time over so many years is still a puzzle.

Bamboo is light, springy and strong for its weight, which makes it a superb building material. In the [[@northeast-india|northeast of India]], many homes are built on bamboo frames. In Hong Kong, workers still put up scaffolding of bamboo poles around [[@skyscrapers|skyscrapers]]. You can see how people build with local materials in [[@homes-world|homes around the world]].

It makes flutes, baskets, mats, bridges and even bicycles. In the 1880s, [[@tesla-edison|Thomas Edison's]] team tested thousands of materials for [[@light-bulb|light bulb]] filaments. A thin strip of baked bamboo from Japan glowed for over a thousand hours, and it was used in Edison's bulbs for years.

sec.h: Food for pandas, homes for many
sec.t:
Giant pandas in China eat almost nothing but bamboo, and the little [[@red-panda|red panda]] of the Himalayas loves it too. In Indian forests, elephants tear down bamboo to munch the leaves, and many birds nest in the thickets.

Because it grows back quickly after cutting, bamboo can replace wood and plastic in many everyday things. Planted on bare slopes, its tangled roots also help hold [[@soil-made|soil]] together during heavy [[monsoon|monsoon]] rain.

text: An air conditioner, or AC, is a heat mover. It works much like a [[@refrigerator|refrigerator]]. Inside the indoor unit, a fan blows warm room air across cold metal coils. A special liquid called a [[refrigerant|refrigerant]] flows through the coils and [[evaporation|evaporates]] there, turning into a gas. Evaporating soaks up heat, so the coils get cold and so does the air blowing past them.

The warm gas then travels through a pipe to the outdoor unit. There, a pump called a compressor squeezes it, making it very hot. A second fan blows outdoor air across a second set of coils, carrying the heat away. The refrigerant cools, turns back into a liquid and flows inside to do it all again. That's why standing next to an outdoor unit on a summer afternoon feels like standing beside an oven.

st.reveal: A simple AC runs at full power until the room reaches the setting, then switches off. Setting it lower doesn't make it work harder. It just keeps running longer, uses more electricity and overshoots. Many newer "inverter" ACs slow down as they near the setting, but a lower number still won't cool faster.

sec.t:
Air always holds some water as an invisible gas. When warm, damp air touches the cold indoor coils, some of that water turns back into droplets, like the drops that form on a cold glass of lassi. The water collects in a tray and drips out through a small pipe.

On a humid day in Chennai or Kolkata, an AC can pull litres of water from a room. Drying the air is a big part of how it makes you comfortable. Your body cools itself by [[@sweat|sweating]], and sweat evaporates far more easily in dry air.

In India, people often describe ACs in tons, such as a 1.5-ton split AC. This has nothing to do with weight. It comes from the days when buildings were cooled with ice. One ton of cooling is the amount of heat needed to melt a ton of ice over 24 hours, roughly 3.5 kilowatts.

India's Bureau of Energy Efficiency gives ACs star ratings, so buyers can see which use less electricity. Since 2020, new ACs sold in India must start at 24 °C unless the user changes it. Each degree warmer saves power. Setting the AC very low doesn't cool the room faster, either. It only makes the machine run for longer, which is one of the most common ways people waste electricity.

Every AC pumps heat out of a room and into the street, and its motor adds more. In crowded cities, thousands of outdoor units make the air outside a little hotter. Power stations that burn coal or gas to run ACs add to [[@climate-change|climate change]], which brings more hot days and more need for cooling.

The International Energy Agency has warned that cooling is one of the fastest-growing uses of electricity in the world. Engineers are working on better refrigerants, smarter buildings with shade and thick walls, and ACs that use far less power.

text: Most lifts in tall buildings hang from strong steel cables. The cables run up to the top of the lift shaft, loop over a big grooved wheel, and come down the other side to a heavy block called a counterweight. An electric motor turns the wheel. Turn it one way and the car rises while the counterweight sinks. Turn it the other way and the car goes down.

The counterweight weighs about as much as the car plus roughly half a full load of passengers. So the motor never has to lift the whole car on its own. It only works against the difference, like pushing one end of a balanced see-saw.
Shorter buildings often use a different kind of lift, pushed up from below by a [[piston|piston]] filled with oil. These are called hydraulic lifts.

st.prompt: In a traction lift, why is there a heavy counterweight on the other end of the cables?

options.t: So the motor only has to lift the difference in weight
To stop the lift from going too high
To keep the cables warm

st.reveal: The counterweight balances the car, like a person on the other end of a see-saw. When the car goes up, the counterweight goes down, and the other way round. The motor only works against the difference, which saves a huge amount of energy.

sec.h: The man who cut the rope
sec.t:
People had used platforms on ropes for centuries, to lift goods in mines and warehouses. But nobody liked riding them. If the rope broke, the platform crashed down.

In 1852, an American mechanic named Elisha Otis invented a safety brake. In 1854, at an exhibition in [[@new-york|New York]], he rode a platform high above the crowd and had the rope cut. The platform dropped only a short way before metal teeth sprang out and locked into the guide rails on either side. Otis is said to have called out, "All safe, gentlemen." The first passenger lift with his brake opened in a New York shop in 1857.

When a lift starts going up, the floor pushes on you a little harder than usual. For a moment, you feel heavier. When it slows down near the top, you feel lighter. Going down, it's the other way round. While the lift moves at a steady speed, you feel completely normal.

This is the same [[gravity|gravity]] and motion that astronauts feel when a [[@rockets-how|rocket]] launches. [[@lifts-skyscraper-speed|The fastest lifts in the world]], in towers in China, travel at about 20 metres a second. That is over 70 km/h, faster than a car on most city roads. They speed up gently and are pressurised so passengers' ears don't hurt too much.

Modern lifts are run by computers. In some tall offices, you tap your floor on a screen in the lobby and it tells you which lift to take. The computer groups people going to nearby floors, so lifts make fewer stops.

Some lifts also save energy. When a heavy car comes down, or a light one goes up, the motor can work as a generator and send electricity back into the building. Very tall towers sometimes use two cars stacked on top of each other in one shaft, stopping at two floors at once.

text: Almost all internet traffic between countries travels through [[@undersea-internet|undersea cables]], not satellites.

Inside, light zooms through glass fibres thinner than a hair. The data is written as rapid flashes of [[@lasers|laser]] light, on and off, standing for the 0s and 1s of [[@binary-code|binary code]]. Light in glass travels about 2 lakh kilometres every second, so it can cross an ocean in a small fraction of a second.
Messages are split into packets that may take different paths, and are joined back together at the end.

sec.t:
When you send a photo, your phone doesn't send it in one piece. It chops it into thousands of small packets. Each one carries a label with where it's going and where it fits in the order, like numbered pages of a letter posted in separate envelopes.

Machines called routers pass the packets along, choosing a free path for each one. If one route is busy or broken, packets go another way. At the other end, the receiving device puts them back in order and asks again for any that went missing. This system was designed in the 1970s by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn in the USA.

More than 500 cables now lie along the [[@ocean-deepest|ocean floor]], joining every continent except Antarctica. In deep water they're about as thick as a garden hose. Near the shore, where they need more protection, they're wrapped in steel and buried under the seabed.

Special ships lay them, unrolling cable as they sail for weeks across the ocean. Cables come ashore at landing stations in places like Mumbai and Chennai, and from there the data runs over land to cities.

[[@sharks-myths|Sharks]] have been filmed biting cables, but they cause very few problems. Most damage comes from ships dragging anchors and from fishing nets. Repair ships fix well over a hundred breaks around the world every year.

{{story:telegraph}}

Sending messages under the sea isn't new. The first cable across the Atlantic was laid in 1858 for the [[@telegraph|telegraph]], [[@morse-to-whatsapp|sending messages in Morse code]]. It worked for only a few weeks before failing, but better cables followed. By the 1870s, a [[telegraph|telegraph]] line linked Britain with India.

Today's cables carry far more. One modern cable can carry enough data for millions of video calls at once. Inside, each glass fibre carries many colours of laser light at the same time, and each colour carries its own stream of data, like separate lanes on one road.

Once the data reaches your town, it travels through fibre or copper cables, or through mobile towers, to your home. The final hop is often [[@wifi|Wi-Fi]], a radio signal from your router to your phone. So a single message might travel as light, as electricity and as [[@radio-waves|radio waves]], all in less than a second.

The delay is still real. A signal going from India to the USA and back takes a noticeable fraction of a second, which is why video calls sometimes have a tiny lag.

The internet doesn't reach space in the same way. Signals to [[@mars-rovers|Mars rovers]] travel by radio and take between about 3 and 22 minutes each way, depending on where the planets are. Even at the speed of light, as you can read in [[@light-years|light-years]], space is big.

text: Coins start as huge rolls of metal sheet, as thick as the coin will be. A machine punches round discs out of the sheet, like a cookie cutter in a kitchen. These plain discs are called blanks.

The blanks are heated to soften them, washed until they shine, and given a raised rim. Then each one goes into a press. Two steel dies, one for each side, slam together with tremendous force and stamp the design into the metal in a fraction of a second. Out drops a finished coin. In India, this happens at four government mints: in Mumbai, Kolkata, Hyderabad and Noida.

st.reveal: When coins were made of silver and gold, crooks shaved thin slivers off the edges and sold the metal. A ridged edge, called reeding, made any shaving easy to spot. Many coins kept the ridges long after they stopped being precious metal.

Most modern coins are cheap metals or alloys. Many Indian coins are ferritic stainless steel. The US penny was about 97.5% zinc with a thin copper coat, and the US "nickel" is mostly copper.

sec.h: The press that never gets tired
sec.t:
Coin presses are fast. Modern ones at the US Mint can strike up to about 750 coins a minute, more than twelve every second. To push the metal into every tiny groove of the design, the dies press with a force of many tonnes. Picture the weight of a loaded truck focused on a disc smaller than your thumbnail.

The metal doesn't melt. It flows, a little like modelling clay squeezed in a mould. That's why the letters on a coin are so crisp. The dies themselves wear out after hundreds of thousands of strikes and must be replaced.

After striking, coins pass over screens and under cameras that pick out bent, cracked or off-centre ones. Rejects are melted down and the metal is used again. The good coins are counted by machine, sealed in bags or boxes, and sent to banks, which pass them on to shops and to you.

The first coins we know of were made about 2,600 years ago in Lydia, in what is now Turkey. They were lumps of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver, stamped with a lion's head.

India has its own early coins. Punch-marked coins of silver, stamped with symbols like the sun, an elephant or a tree, were used across the Ganga plains from about 2,500 years ago, including in the [[@mauryan-empire|Mauryan Empire]]. Rather than one design, each coin got several separate punches, like rubber stamps.

Have a look at a coin's edge. The ridges there have a history. In the 1600s, people clipped silver from coin edges. In England, [[@newton-life|Isaac Newton]] became warden of the Royal Mint in 1696 and hunted forgers and clippers himself. Coins with ridged or lettered edges made clipping easy to spot.

Holes have a purpose too. Coins with holes, used in China for about 2,000 years and in places like Japan today, could be strung together. In 2019, India released coins with different shapes and sizes so that people who are blind can tell them apart by touch. And if you drop one on a beach, its metal is exactly what a [[@metal-detectors|metal detector]] is listening for.

text: भारत लगभग किसी भी देश से ज़्यादा फ़िल्में बनाता है, और उनमें से ज़्यादातर में गाने होते हैं। संगीतकार, जिसे अक्सर म्यूज़िक डायरेक्टर कहते हैं, ये गाने और पीछे बजने वाला संगीत रचता है। सौ सालों में कुछ गिने-चुने संगीतकारों ने तय किया है कि भारत कैसा "सुनाई" देता है।

sec.t:
1931 में भारत की पहली बोलती फ़िल्म *आलम आरा* सात गानों के साथ आई। तब से संगीत भारतीय फ़िल्मों का दिल रहा है। 1950 और 60 के दशक को अक्सर हिंदी फ़िल्म संगीत का सुनहरा दौर कहा जाता है।

नौशाद ने हिंदुस्तानी शास्त्रीय संगीत से गहराई से रस लिया। *मुग़ल-ए-आज़म* (1960) के लिए उन्होंने बड़े गायक-दलों और ऑर्केस्ट्रा के साथ [[@raga-time|रागों]] पर टिके भव्य गाने बनाए। त्रिपुरा के एक राजघराने से आए एस. डी. बर्मन बंगाल की लोक धुनें और वहाँ की नदियों के माँझियों के गीत लेकर आए। सलिल चौधरी ने अपने प्रिय पश्चिमी शास्त्रीय संगीत से प्रेरणा लेकर बांग्ला लोक संगीत में पश्चिमी हार्मनी घोली। इनमें से बहुत-से गाने [[@lata-mangeshkar|लता मंगेशकर]] ने गाए, जिनकी आवाज़ भारत के लगभग हर घर तक पहुँची।

sec.h: गाँव का लड़का और एक सिम्फ़नी
sec.t:
तमिलनाडु में इलैयाराजा पन्नैपुरम गाँव में अपने भाइयों के साथ लोकगीत गाते हुए बड़े हुए। बाद में उन्होंने पश्चिमी शास्त्रीय संगीत सीखा और दोनों के उस्ताद बन गए। संगीतकार के रूप में उनकी पहली फ़िल्म 1976 में आई।

आगे चलकर उन्होंने लगभग 1,000 फ़िल्मों का संगीत रचा, ज़्यादातर तमिल, तेलुगु, कन्नड़ और मलयालम में। अक्सर वे हर साज़ का हिस्सा खुद, तेज़ी से और हाथ से लिखते थे। 2025 में उन्होंने लंदन में अपनी सिम्फ़नी पहली बार पेश की। उनके काम ने [[@cinema-south|दक्षिण भारतीय सिनेमा]] को उसके संगीत के लिए मशहूर करने में मदद की।

sec.h: 1990 के दशक और उसके बाद की आवाज़
sec.t:
1992 में चेन्नई के एक नौजवान कीबोर्ड वादक, [[@ar-rahman|ए. आर. रहमान]], ने तमिल फ़िल्म *रोजा* का संगीत बनाया। यह पहले की किसी भी चीज़ जैसा नहीं था, जिसमें साफ़-सुथरी इलेक्ट्रॉनिक थापें, लोक आवाज़ें और भरी-पूरी, निखरी हुई [[sound|ध्वनि]] थी। इसके गाने पूरे भारत में हिट हुए।

आगे चलकर 2009 में रहमान ने *स्लमडॉग मिलियनेयर* के लिए दो ऑस्कर जीते। 2023 में एम. एम. कीरवाणी ने तेलुगु फ़िल्म *आरआरआर* के नाच वाले गाने "नाटू नाटू" के लिए ऑस्कर जीता। इसकी तेज़, धमधमाती थाप पर हैदराबाद से लॉस एंजेलिस तक सिनेमाघरों में लोग नाच उठे।

संगीतकार शायद ही कभी अकेले काम करता है। निर्देशक दृश्य समझाता है, जैसे कोई शादी, पीछा या दुख भरी विदाई। संगीतकार कोई धुन गुनगुनाता या बजाता है, गीतकार बोल लिखता है, और अरेंजर तय करता है कि कौन सा साज़ कब बजेगा। पुराने ज़माने में दर्जनों साज़िंदे एक स्टूडियो में ठसाठस बैठकर साथ रिकॉर्ड करते थे, इसलिए एक गलती का मतलब था सब कुछ शुरू से।

ऐसी सूचियों में हमेशा कुछ लोग छूट जाते हैं। शंकर-जयकिशन ने राज कपूर की फ़िल्मों के लिए दर्जनों हिट गाने बनाए। लक्ष्मीकांत-प्यारेलाल की जोड़ी ने लगभग 35 सालों में सैकड़ों फ़िल्मों पर काम किया। 1930 के दशक में सरस्वती देवी बॉम्बे टॉकीज़ में हिंदी फ़िल्मों के लिए संगीत रचने वाली पहली महिलाओं में से एक बनीं। हर भाषा के अपने नायक हैं, तमिल में एम. एस. विश्वनाथन से लेकर बांग्ला में हेमंत कुमार तक।

sec.t:
मेहँदी के डिज़ाइन [[motif|मोटिफ़ों]] से भरे होते हैं, यानी छोटे-छोटे आकार जो बार-बार दोहराए जाते हैं। मोर, कमल, कैरी के आकार की बूटियाँ (पैस्ली), बेलें, बिंदियाँ और बारीक रेखाओं की जालियाँ अक्सर दिखती हैं। अच्छे कलाकार [[@symmetry|सममिति]] का इस्तेमाल करते हैं, यानी दोनों तरफ़ आकारों को आईने की तरह दोहराते हैं, ताकि पूरा डिज़ाइन संतुलित लगे।

कई इलाकाई शैलियाँ हैं। राजस्थानी मेहँदी अक्सर पूरे हाथ और बाँह को बहुत बारीक काम से ढक देती है, कभी-कभी दूल्हा-दुल्हन की आकृतियों के साथ। अरबी शैली में बड़े फूल और पत्तियाँ होती हैं, जो हाथ पर तिरछी बेल की तरह चलती हैं और ज़्यादा त्वचा खाली छोड़ती हैं। इंडो-अरबी डिज़ाइन दोनों को मिला देते हैं।

बहुत-से भारतीय परिवारों में शादी से एक-दो दिन पहले दुल्हन की मेहँदी की रस्म होती है। रिश्तेदार और सहेलियाँ जुटती हैं, गीत गाती हैं और अपने हाथों पर भी मेहँदी लगवाती हैं। एक मशहूर खेल है दुल्हन के डिज़ाइन में दूल्हे का नाम या उसके पहले अक्षर छिपा देना, और फिर दूल्हे को उन्हें ढूँढना पड़ता है।

मेहँदी अलग-अलग धर्मों और इलाकों के बहुत-से उत्सवों का हिस्सा है। महिलाएँ और लड़कियाँ इसे [[@eid|ईद]], करवा चौथ, तीज और दिवाली पर लगाती हैं, और भारत, पाकिस्तान, बांग्लादेश, खाड़ी देशों और उत्तरी अफ़्रीका में [[@weddings-india|शादियों]] पर भी। कई जगह माना जाता है कि गहरी रची मेहँदी सौभाग्य या प्यार की निशानी है। शायद इसीलिए लोग लेप इतनी देर तक लगाए रखते हैं।

लेप हट जाने के बहुत देर बाद तक रंग गहराता रहता है। लॉसोन तुम्हारी त्वचा की कोशिकाओं के केराटिन से चिपक जाता है, और वहाँ टिककर धीरे-धीरे हवा की ऑक्सीजन से क्रिया करता है। इस क्रिया को [[oxidation|ऑक्सीकरण]] कहते हैं। इसी से लगभग 24 से 48 घंटों में रंग चटख नारंगी से गहरे लाल-भूरे की ओर खिसकता है।

गर्माहट से रंग अंदर तक सोखने में मदद मिलती है। इसीलिए कुछ लोग लेप सूखने के बाद हाथों को गर्म चाय के कप के पास रखते हैं। ताज़ा मेहँदी पाउडर पुराने पाउडर से गहरा रंग देता है, क्योंकि समय के साथ लॉसोन टूटता जाता है। जो हाथ बार-बार धोए जाते हैं या साबुन से रगड़े जाते हैं, उनका रंग जल्दी उतरता है, क्योंकि रंगी हुई बाहरी कोशिकाएँ घिसकर निकल जाती हैं।

लोग हज़ारों सालों से मेहँदी इस्तेमाल करते आए हैं। प्राचीन मिस्र की कुछ [[@mummies|ममियों]] के बाल या नाखून नारंगी-लाल रँगे मिले हैं, और शोधकर्ता मानते हैं कि यह रंग मेहँदी का है। इससे बाल, नाखून, चमड़ा, और घोड़ों के अयाल और पूँछ तक रँगे गए हैं।

मेहँदी त्वचा को ठंडक भी देती है। हो सकता है यह भी एक वजह हो कि गर्म इलाकों में यह इतनी लोकप्रिय हुई। गहरा रंग पाने के लिए धीरज चाहिए। मेहँदी लगाने वाले सलाह देते हैं कि लेप कई घंटे लगा रहने दो, उसे नम रखने के लिए ऊपर से नींबू-चीनी का घोल थपथपाते रहो, और पहले दिन पानी से बचो। उसके बाद बस इंतज़ार करना है कि नारंगी रंग लाल-भूरा हो जाए।

text: A charity is an organisation set up to help people, animals or the environment, rather than to make a profit. Charities collect money, food, clothes and time from donors and volunteers, and use them to run schools, feed hungry people, care for the sick, rescue animals, or help after floods and earthquakes.

Some charities are tiny, like a group of neighbours running a free tuition class. Others are huge and work in dozens of countries. The best ones study what people really need, work alongside them, and check whether their help is making a difference.

sec.t:
Almost every culture and religion encourages giving. In Hinduism, *daan* means giving without expecting anything back. Sikh gurdwaras run *langar*, free community kitchens that serve anyone who comes, whatever their background. The langar at [[@golden-temple|the Golden Temple]] in Amritsar feeds tens of thousands of people a day.

In Islam, *zakat*, usually 2.5% of a person's savings each year, is one of the five pillars of faith. Many Muslims also give to the poor before [[@eid|Eid]]. In Christianity and Judaism, there is a long tradition of giving a tenth of one's income.

In 1859, a Swiss businessman named Henri Dunant saw thousands of wounded soldiers left without care after a battle in Italy. His ideas led to the founding of [[@red-cross|the Red Cross]] in 1863. Today the Red Cross and Red Crescent help people in conflicts and disasters worldwide.

Other charities focus on one problem. [[@kailash-satyarthi|Kailash Satyarthi]], who shared the [[@nobel-peace|Nobel Peace Prize]] in 2014, founded a movement that has rescued thousands of children from forced labour in India.

One famous test came from economists Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo, who studied ways to fight poverty in India and elsewhere by running careful experiments, much like testing a medicine. They shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in economics with Michael Kremer for this work, and many charities now use similar methods.

Good intentions are not enough. Sometimes donations of old clothes or food arrive where they are not needed, or hurt local sellers. So many charities now test their work, comparing places that receive help with places that do not.

People also argue about charity itself. Some say it can never replace fair laws and good government. Others point out that charities often reach people that governments miss. Even famous figures are debated. [[@mother-teresa|Mother Teresa]], who cared for the dying in Kolkata, is admired by millions, while some critics questioned the medical care in her homes. Most people agree that giving, done thoughtfully, can change lives.

text: A [[constitution|constitution]] is a country's highest set of rules. Because it matters so much, it is deliberately hard to change. Each change is called an [[amendment|amendment]].

Most countries require a bigger majority than for ordinary laws. In India, most amendments need a two-thirds majority of members present and voting in each house of Parliament, and some also need approval from half the state legislatures. In the USA, an amendment needs two-thirds of both houses of Congress, and then three-quarters of the 50 states must agree. Some countries, like Ireland and Switzerland, put changes to a public vote, a [[referendum|referendum]].

sec.t:
In 1982, Gregory Watson, a student at the University of Texas, wrote a paper about an amendment first proposed by James Madison in 1789. It said that if members of Congress voted themselves a pay rise, it couldn't take effect until after the next election. The amendment had never been ratified by enough states, but it had no deadline.

Watson's teacher gave him a C. He began writing to state lawmakers across the country, asking them to ratify it. One by one, they did. In 1992, the 27th Amendment became part of the Constitution, more than 200 years after it was proposed. In 2017, the university changed his grade to an A.

India's [[@constitution|Constitution]] is much longer and more detailed than America's, so it needs changing more often. Its makers expected this. In the [[@constituent-assembly|Constituent Assembly]], B. R. Ambedkar argued that each generation should be able to adapt the Constitution to its own needs, so India chose a path between very rigid and very easy. The 1st Amendment came in 1951. The 61st, in 1988, lowered the voting age from 21 to 18. The 73rd, in 1992, made [[@panchayat|panchayats]] a part of the Constitution. The 86th, in 2002, made education a fundamental right for children aged 6 to 14. The 106th, in 2023, reserved a third of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies for women, to take effect after the next [[census|census]] and redrawing of constituencies.

The 42nd Amendment of 1976, passed during [[@emergency-1975|the Emergency]], made so many changes that it was called a "mini-constitution". It added the words "socialist" and "secular" to the Preamble. Many of its other changes were reversed in 1978.

Can an amendment change anything at all? In 1973, in a case brought by Kesavananda Bharati, the head of a [[monastery|monastery]] in Kerala, the Supreme Court of India said no. [[parliament|Parliament]] can amend the Constitution, the judges ruled, but not destroy its "basic structure", such as democracy, federalism, secularism and judicial review.

The decision was close, seven judges to six. It remains one of the most important judgments in Indian history, and courts in some other countries have since borrowed the idea.

text: People build homes from whatever is nearby and whatever the weather demands. In the Arctic, it has been snow. In the Mongolian grasslands, felt and wooden poles. In the Assam floodplains, bamboo raised on stilts. In the Thar desert, mud and cow dung that keep rooms cool.

There are homes that float, homes that move, homes underground and homes hanging off cliffs. Many look strange to outsiders, but each one is a clever answer to a local problem. In crowded cities, most people now live in flats and apartments, in towers that can hold more people than a whole village.

sec.t:
In Coober Pedy, a small town in the Australian outback, summer days often go above 40 °C. Many people there live in "dugouts", homes carved into the hillside rock. The rock keeps the inside around 23 to 25 °C all year, with no air conditioner. The town even has underground churches and a hotel.

In Matmata, Tunisia, families dug pit homes into the ground, with rooms opening onto a round courtyard. One was used as Luke Skywalker's home in the first Star Wars film in 1977, and fans still visit. Underground homes are among the oldest ideas in housing, a story that runs back to the [[@cave-to-houses|first shelters]] humans ever made.

On Dal Lake in Srinagar, hundreds of carved wooden houseboats float near the shore. A story often told is that, under Dogra rule, British visitors weren't allowed to buy land in Kashmir, so they built homes on the water instead. Many houseboats now take tourists.

In Kerala, the *kettuvallam*, once a rice barge, has become a floating holiday home. The Bajau people of South-East Asia have lived on boats and stilt houses over the sea for centuries. Some Bajau divers can hold their breath for minutes at a time while fishing.

The igloo is famous, but it was mainly a short-stay shelter. Inuit hunters could build one from blocks of packed snow in an hour or two. Snow is full of tiny air pockets, so it traps heat well.

In Assam, the Mising people build *chang ghar*, bamboo houses on stilts, to stay dry when the Brahmaputra floods. In the Nilgiri hills, the Toda people built barrel-shaped huts of bamboo and grass with a door so small you crawl in, keeping heat inside.

Before electric fans, homes in hot places used tricks. Thick mud walls soak up heat in the day and release it at night. Courtyards pull in breezes. In old Gujarat and Rajasthan houses, jaalis, carved stone screens, let air in while blocking sun. Some homes hang wet cloths in doorways, so moving air cools as water dries, the same science as [[@evaporation-cooling|evaporation cooling]].

Clay, mud and burnt brick remain among the world's most common walls. Fired [[@bricks|bricks]] were already being used in the cities of the Indus Valley more than 4,000 years ago.

text: A street vendor runs a tiny business on a cart, a basket, a cloth on the pavement or a bicycle. The plan is simple. Buy goods cheaply early in the morning, carry them to where people are, sell them at a small profit, and do it again tomorrow.

Simple does not mean easy. A vendor must choose the right spot, guess how much to buy, set prices that beat the shop down the road and keep regulars coming back. All of this happens with almost no savings to fall back on. Many families in India depend on it. Estimates of how many street vendors India has usually start at about 1 crore and go much higher.

st.prompt: A vendor borrows ₹1,000 in the morning to buy vegetables and must pay back ₹1,100 by evening. If this happened every working day, how much extra would she pay in a month of 25 days?
st.reveal: She pays ₹100 extra each day, so 25 days cost ₹2,500, more than double what she borrowed. Daily loans like this from moneylenders are one reason small, cheap bank loans for vendors matter so much.

sec.h: A day that starts in the dark
sec.t:
A vegetable seller's day often begins around 4 or 5 in the morning at a wholesale market, called a mandi. Prices are lowest there, but only if you buy in bulk and bargain hard. By 7 she is at her spot, arranging tomatoes in neat pyramids so they look fresh.

Food vendors work differently. A pani puri seller may spend the afternoon at home frying hundreds of puris and boiling potatoes, then sell from 5 to 10 at night. Every vendor plays the same guessing game. Buy too little and you run out by noon. Buy too much and fruit rots, which can wipe out a day's profit. Prices follow [[@supply-demand|supply and demand]]: when everyone has mangoes, mangoes are cheap.

A vendor's location is their shop window. A cart outside a school, a railway station or an office gate sees hundreds of hungry people a day. Moving even one street away can halve sales.

Vada pav, Mumbai's famous potato burger, is often said to have been made popular by a stall near Dadar station in the 1960s. It worked because it was fast, filling and cheap, right where crowds of mill workers passed.

Regular customers matter too. Many vendors remember who likes extra chutney or less chilli. Some even let trusted buyers pay later.

{{story:upi-payments}}

Most vendors have little spare cash. In the past, many borrowed from moneylenders who charged huge interest, sometimes ₹100 a day on a ₹1,000 loan. Over a month, that is far more than the loan itself. You can see how quickly [[@money-interest-loans|interest]] adds up.

In 2020, the Indian government started PM SVANidhi, a scheme offering small loans without asking for property as security. By 2026, more than 75 lakh vendors had taken over 1 crore loans, and nearly half the borrowers were women.

Phones changed things too. Thanks to [[@upi-payments|UPI]], a printed QR code costs almost nothing, so even a chaiwala can accept digital payments. Paying by phone also builds a record, which helps vendors show a bank they have a steady income.

Vendors often clash with city officials over space on crowded pavements. India passed the Street Vendors Act in 2014. It says cities should count their vendors, issue them certificates and set up vending zones with local committees.

The fight over pavement space happens in the USA too. New York City capped the number of food cart permits at about 5,000 for nearly 40 years, so many vendors waited years or rented permits from others. New laws in 2021 and 2026 began adding thousands more. Some American cities now celebrate their carts with awards and festivals.

There is a quiet cleverness in all of it. A good vendor reads the weather, the season and the crowd better than any app. And the snack with the longest queue on many Indian streets is [[@pani-puri|pani puri]], a crisp ball of spicy water with a different name in almost every city.

text: Volunteering means giving your time and effort to help others, without being paid. Volunteers teach children to read, plant trees, serve food, clean beaches, help at hospitals, rescue animals and assist after disasters. Some give an hour a month, and some give years.

People volunteer for many reasons: to help a cause they care about, to meet people, to learn skills or to give something back to their community. Many organisations, from small local groups to huge international [[@charity|charities]], would struggle to work without volunteers.

Children can volunteer in many ways, usually with a parent, teacher or youth group. Scouts and Guides, school eco-clubs and online science projects all welcome young volunteers.

sec.t:
Some volunteers do serious, risky jobs. In the United States, about two in three [[@jobs-firefighter|firefighters]] are volunteers, especially in small towns where there are not enough emergencies to pay a full-time crew. They train for many hours and leave work or bed when the alarm sounds.

In India, the National Service Scheme was launched in 1969, the centenary year of [[@gandhi|Gandhi]]'s birth. College and higher-secondary students in the scheme spend time on community work, such as health camps, literacy drives and cleanliness campaigns. Millions have taken part. The [[@scouts-guides|Scouts and Guides]] movement also trains young people to help others.

You do not have to leave home to volunteer. Through "citizen science" projects, ordinary people help researchers by counting birds, recording rainfall or sorting photos.

In 2007, a Dutch schoolteacher named Hanny van Arkel was classifying photos of [[@galaxies|galaxies]] for an online project called Galaxy Zoo. She noticed a strange green blob next to one [[galaxy|galaxy]]. [[astronomer|Astronomers]] studied it and found a huge glowing gas cloud, now known as Hanny's Voorwerp, Dutch for "Hanny's object". Volunteers in projects like this have helped discover new planets around other stars too.

{{story:galaxies}}

Birdwatchers around the world, including many in India, record what they see in online databases. Scientists use these records to track bird [[@migration|migration]] and how populations change.

Some of the world's biggest environmental movements were led by volunteers. In the 1970s, villagers in the Himalayan foothills, many of them women, protected their forests by hugging trees to stop them being cut, in what became known as the [[@chipko|Chipko movement]]. Across India, groups of volunteers now clean beaches, revive lakes and plant saplings on weekends.

The US Peace Corps, founded in 1961, sends American volunteers to live and work in other countries for two years, teaching, farming or supporting health projects. Other countries run similar programmes. The United Nations has its own volunteer service, and since 1985 it has marked 5 December as International Volunteer Day.

In emergencies, volunteers often arrive before anyone else. After floods in [[@kerala|Kerala]] in 2018, fishermen took their own boats into flooded towns and rescued thousands of people. Students and neighbours ran relief camps, cooked meals and sorted donations. Volunteers also help run huge gatherings like the Kumbh Mela, guiding pilgrims and reuniting lost family members.

Volunteering is unpaid, but people often say they gain a lot: new friends, new skills and a sense of purpose. Studies find that people who volunteer tend to report feeling happier, though it is hard to tell how much volunteering causes that. You can read more about this in [[@kindness-science|Is kindness good for you?]]. For young people, volunteering can also be a way to try out a kind of work before choosing a career.

text: A map is a drawing of a place made much smaller, so it fits on paper or a screen. The scale tells you how much smaller.

A scale might say 1:50,000. That means 1 centimetre on the map stands for 50,000 centimetres on the ground, which is 500 metres. Many maps also have a little bar with marks showing 1 km or 1 mile, so you can measure distances with a ruler or a piece of string.

The bigger the second number, the more the world has been shrunk. A street map of your town might be 1:10,000. A map of all of India in a school atlas might be 1:1,50,00,000 or smaller. Shrinking a [[@what-if-earth-flat|round Earth]] onto flat paper also bends some shapes, which causes trouble on world maps.

st.prompt: On a map with a scale of 1:1,00,000, two towns are 5 cm apart. How far apart are they really?

options.t: 500 metres
5 kilometres
50 kilometres

st.reveal: A scale of 1:1,00,000 means every centimetre on the map stands for 1,00,000 cm on the ground. That's 1,000 metres, or 1 km. So 5 cm on the map is 5 km in real life.

myth: Greenland is about the same size as Africa.
It only looks that way on maps using the Mercator projection, which stretches places near the poles. Africa is really about 14 times bigger than Greenland.

sec.t:
Mapmakers choose a scale depending on what the map is for. A hiking map needs every path and stream, so it uses a large scale, where a small area fills the page. A world map shows only big things like countries and oceans, so it uses a tiny scale.

A scale is really a [[@fractions|fraction]]. A scale of 1:50,000 means the map is 1/50,000 the size of the land. Zooming in on a phone map is like switching between scales in an instant.

In 1802, a British army officer named William Lambton began one of the greatest measuring projects ever attempted: the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. Starting near Madras, now [[@chennai|Chennai]], his teams measured a base line along the ground with great care. Then they measured the angles from hilltops and towers to distant points, building chains of [[@shapes-angles|triangles]] across the land.

After Lambton died in 1823, George Everest took over. The teams worked for decades, through jungles and heat and illness. The central line, called the Great Arc, ran about 2,500 km from near Kanyakumari in the far south up to the Himalayas.

The Earth is round, and paper is flat. Turning one into the other always stretches or squashes something. The different ways of doing it are called projections.

In 1569, the Flemish mapmaker Gerardus Mercator made a world map for sailors. On his map, a straight line is a constant compass direction, which made it very useful for [[navigation|navigation]]. But it stretches land near the poles. Greenland looks as big as Africa, when Africa is about 14 times bigger. Many people still picture the world this way.

Modern maps are made from satellite photos and measurements. [[@gps-how|GPS]] [[@satellites-help|satellites]] let surveyors fix positions to within centimetres. The Survey of India, founded in 1767, is one of the oldest scientific departments in the country and still makes official maps.

Maps can never show everything. The writer Lewis Carroll joked about a country that made a map at a scale of a mile to the mile, the same size as the land itself. Farmers complained it would cover the fields and block the sunlight, so they used the country itself as its own map instead.

text: Dhundiraj Govind Phalke, known as Dadasaheb Phalke, is called the father of Indian cinema. In 1913 he made *Raja Harishchandra*, the first full-length Indian feature film. It told the story of a truthful king from Indian legend, and it was silent, with title cards in Marathi and Hindi.

Phalke went on to make about 95 feature films and 26 short ones, mostly stories of gods and heroes. He built a studio, trained actors and camera operators, and invented his own tricks for special effects. India's highest award for cinema is named after him.

A famous stage actress from Calcutta

st.reveal: Acting in films was thought unrespectable for women in 1913. After failing to find an actress, Phalke cast Anna Salunke, a young man who worked in a restaurant. In his very next film, Mohini Bhasmasur, made later in 1913, Durgabai Kamat and her daughter Kamlabai became the first women to act in Indian films.

sec.t:
Phalke was born in 1870 in Trimbak, a temple town near Nashik, where his father was a Sanskrit scholar. He studied art in Bombay and Baroda, then tried a string of jobs. He was a photographer, a stage-set painter, a magician and a printer who made coloured pictures.

On stage he called himself Professor Kelpha, a jumbled-up version of his own surname, and he had learned the magic from a German conjuror touring India.

That mix turned out to be the perfect training for a filmmaker. He understood light, chemicals, painting, printing and illusion. He just had not yet seen what to do with them.

sec.h: The film that changed his life

sec.t:
Back in [[@mumbai|Bombay]], his home became a studio. His wife, Saraswatibai, helped develop film, fed the cast and crew, and sold her jewellery when money ran short. Their children helped too. In a later film, *Kaliya Mardan* (1919), their daughter Mandakini played the [[@myths-krishna-childhood|young Krishna]].

Finding actors was hard. No respectable woman would act in a film in 1913, so the queen in *Raja Harishchandra* was played by a young man, Anna Salunke. The film, about 40 minutes long, opened to the public on 3 May 1913 at the Coronation Cinema in Bombay. Audiences came back again and again.

Phalke's mythological films were full of magic. Gods appeared out of smoke, demons vanished and heroes flew. He made them with double exposures, models and careful editing, years before most filmmakers in India had heard of such things. His later films, such as *Lanka Dahan* (1917), drew some of the biggest crowds Indian cinemas had yet seen. Today's [[@special-effects|special effects]] use computers, but the aim is the same.

When sound films arrived in the 1930s, Phalke's style fell out of fashion. He made only one talkie, *Gangavataran*, in 1937. He died in Nashik in 1944, without much money and largely forgotten by the industry he had started.

In 1969, the Government of India created the Dadasaheb Phalke Award for lifetime achievement in cinema. The first winner was the actress Devika Rani. Later winners include [[@satyajit-ray|Satyajit Ray]], Lata Mangeshkar and Raj Kapoor. Every Indian film, from a Tamil blockbuster to a Bengali art film, traces its family tree back to a printer with a camera and a pot of peas.

text: India's Olympic heroes include the hockey teams that won eight gold medals. [[@shooting-sport|Shooter]] Abhinav Bindra won India's first individual gold in 2008, and javelin thrower [[@neeraj-chopra|Neeraj Chopra]] became the first Indian to win gold in athletics. [[@wrestling-india|Wrestlers]], boxers, badminton players, weightlifters and shooters have all added medals.

India has won about 41 medals at the Summer [[@olympics|Olympics]]. That is few for a country of its size, but the number has grown fast. India won 7 medals at Tokyo, its best ever, and 6 in Paris in 2024.

sec.t:
From 1928 to 1956, India's men's hockey team won six Olympic golds in a row, led at first by the great [[@dhyan-chand|Dhyan Chand]]. They won again in 1964 and 1980.

The 1948 gold in London, won by beating Great Britain in the final, was India's first as an independent nation. For decades hockey was almost the only sport in which India won Olympic medals. After 1980 the team waited 41 years for another, a bronze at Tokyo.

Two of India's best-loved athletes never won an Olympic medal. At Rome in 1960, [[@milkha-singh|Milkha Singh]], the "Flying Sikh", finished fourth in the 400 metres. At Los Angeles in 1984, P. T. Usha finished fourth in the 400 metres hurdles, just one hundredth of a second behind the bronze medallist.

Both went on to inspire generations of runners, and their stories are still told in films and schoolbooks.

On 11 August 2008 in Beijing, Abhinav Bindra won the 10 metre air rifle event, India's first individual gold. London 2012 brought six medals, including bronzes for boxer [[@mary-kom|Mary Kom]] and [[@badminton|badminton]] player Saina Nehwal.

In Rio in 2016, India's only medals came from two women: badminton player [[@pv-sindhu|P. V. Sindhu]] won silver and wrestler Sakshi Malik won bronze. Sindhu added a bronze in Tokyo, becoming the first Indian woman with two individual Olympic medals.

In Tokyo, at Games held in 2021, weightlifter Mirabai Chanu won silver on the first day. On 7 August, Neeraj Chopra threw the javelin 87.58 metres to win gold. A javelin flies furthest when it leaves the hand at the right angle and speed, a contest between the thrower's strength and [[@gravity-fall|gravity]].

At Paris 2024, shooter Manu Bhaker won two bronze medals, one alone and one in a mixed team event with Sarabjot Singh. She became the first Indian to win two medals at a single Olympics since independence. Neeraj won silver, the hockey team won bronze, and wrestler Aman Sehrawat and shooter Swapnil Kusale added bronzes.

India's athletes also shine at the [[@paralympics|Paralympics]], where India won 29 medals in Paris. With better training centres and support, many Indian fans hope the next generation will turn fourth places into podiums.

text: Raj Kapoor was one of the most loved actors and filmmakers in Indian cinema. Between the late 1940s and the 1980s, he acted in, directed and produced films that mixed comedy, romance, music and big questions about rich and poor.

His most famous character was a cheerful, penniless wanderer, a little like Charlie Chaplin's Tramp, with baggy trousers, a battered hat and a big heart. Films such as *Awaara* (1951) and *Shree 420* (1955) made him a star in India and across the Soviet Union, the Middle East and parts of Asia and Africa. People called him "the showman" of Hindi cinema.

sec.t:
Raj Kapoor was born in 1924 in Peshawar, then part of British India, now in Pakistan. His father, Prithviraj Kapoor, was a famous stage and film actor who later moved the family to Bombay. Young Raj worked as a clapper boy and assistant on film sets, sweeping floors and holding the board that marks each shot.

He started acting as a child and got his first lead role in 1947. A year later, aged 24, he founded his own company, R. K. Films. The Kapoors went on to become one of the best-known families in Indian cinema, with his sons, grandchildren and great-grandchildren acting in films.

During the [[@cold-war|Cold War]], the Soviet government allowed few Western films. Indian films, with their stories about the struggles of ordinary people, were welcome. *Awaara* was released there in 1954 and drew huge audiences. Raj Kapoor was mobbed by fans on his visits.

For many Soviet citizens, India meant Raj Kapoor and his songs. Even today, older Russians, Uzbeks and others sometimes greet Indian visitors by humming "Awaara Hoon".

Raj Kapoor's films are remembered as much for their songs as their stories. He worked again and again with the same team: the composers Shankar and Jaikishan, the lyricists Shailendra and Hasrat Jaipuri, the playback singer Mukesh, who sang for him, and [[@lata-mangeshkar|Lata Mangeshkar]]. Many of their [[@film-songs|film songs]] are still played at weddings and on radio.

He often acted with Nargis, and their pairing in films such as *Barsaat* and *Shree 420* is one of the most famous in Indian cinema.

Not every film succeeded. *Mera Naam Joker* (1970), about a circus clown, was long and expensive and flopped at first, leaving him in debt. He bounced back with *Bobby* (1973), a teenage love story that launched a new generation of young romantic heroes.

Critics have pointed out that some of his later films leaned on glamour more than storytelling. Still, he won many awards, including the Dadasaheb Phalke Award for 1987. He fell seriously ill at the ceremony in May 1988 and died a month later. In 2024, India marked his 100th birthday with festivals of his films. *Mera Naam Joker* is now seen as a classic, and its circus scenes are still shown to film students.

text: Swimmers go fast by pushing a lot of water backwards while letting as little water as possible push back against them. That push-back is called [[drag|drag]]. Water is about 800 times denser than air, so drag matters far more in a pool than on a running track.

Top swimmers keep their bodies long, straight and flat, like an arrow. They use their arms and legs as paddles, kick powerfully underwater after every start and turn, and wear tight caps and suits. A world-class swimmer can reach about 8 km an hour, roughly a brisk jog.

st.prompt: Top swimmers can be faster underwater than on the surface. Why?

options.t: Waves at the surface create extra drag
Water is thinner below the surface
They can hold their breath, which makes them lighter

st.reveal: At the surface, a swimmer pushes up waves that waste energy. Underwater, with a strong dolphin kick, there are no waves. That is why rules limit how far swimmers may travel underwater after a start or turn.

myth: You must wait an hour after eating before swimming, or you will get a cramp and drown.

Reviews by safety experts, including the American Red Cross, found no evidence for this. A huge meal might feel uncomfortable, but a normal snack is fine. Always swim where an adult or lifeguard is watching.

sec.t:
Drag comes in a few forms. Some comes from the shape of the body pushing water aside, which is why swimmers stretch out with arms over their heads. Some comes from water rubbing along the skin, a kind of [[@friction|friction]]. Some comes from waves the swimmer makes at the surface.

Good technique cuts all three. Swimmers rotate their bodies to slice through the water and keep their heads low. Some shave body hair before big races. Studies suggest this reduces drag slightly and makes the water feel smoother.

A fast pool is part of the secret. Olympic pools are 50 metres long and deep, which keeps waves from bouncing off the bottom. Lane ropes have spinning discs that break up waves, and gutters at the edges soak up the splashes.

Swimmers save time with tumble turns and long underwater kicks. Because underwater swimming was becoming so fast, rules now limit it to 15 metres after each start or turn.

Around 2008, new swimsuits made of polyurethane trapped air and squeezed swimmers into a smooth shape. Some designs were inspired by [[@sharks-old|shark skin]], which has tiny ridges. In 2008 and 2009 over 100 [[@world-records|world records]] fell. Many said the suits, not the swimmers, were winning races.

From 2010, full-body suits were banned. Men's suits may now reach only from waist to knee, and women's from shoulder to knee.

Michael Phelps of the USA won eight gold medals at the 2008 Beijing [[@olympics|Olympics]] and 23 Olympic golds in total. His arm span, about 2.01 metres, is longer than his height of about 1.93 metres. Long arms and large feet work like big oars and flippers.

Indians have made swimming history too. In 1958 Mihir Sen became the first Asian to [[@body-cold-swimmers|swim the English Channel]] between England and France. In 1959 Arati Saha became the first Asian woman to do it. In 2021 Sajan Prakash and Srihari Nataraj became the first Indian swimmers to reach the strict "A" qualifying time for the Olympics. sec.t:
बची हुई सबसे पुरानी चिकित्सा-पोथियों में से एक है [[@ancient-egypt|प्राचीन मिस्र]] का एडविन स्मिथ पेपिरस, जिसे लगभग 1600 ईसा पूर्व में और भी पुराने लेखों से उतारा गया था। इसमें सिर के घावों से लेकर टूटी हड्डियों तक, चोटों के 48 मामलों का ब्योरा है, और यह भी कि उनकी जाँच और इलाज कैसे करें। इसमें यह तक लिखा है कि दिमाग की चोट शरीर के किसी दूर के हिस्से पर असर डाल सकती है।

भारत की सुश्रुत संहिता में शल्य-चिकित्सा के बहुत-से औज़ारों और ऑपरेशनों का वर्णन है, जिनमें गाल की त्वचा से खराब हुई नाक को ठीक करना भी शामिल है। यह कब लिखी गई, इस पर इतिहासकार एकमत नहीं हैं, पर यह सदियों में बढ़ती गई और इसके कुछ हिस्से 2,000 साल से भी पुराने हैं। [[@sushruta|सुश्रुत]] को अक्सर शल्य-चिकित्सा का एक पितामह कहा जाता है। [[@ayurveda-yoga|आयुर्वेद]] का ग्रंथ चरक संहिता खान-पान, बीमारी और दवाइयों के बारे में बताता है।

sec.h: यूनानी विचार और एक लंबी भूल

sec.t:
1543 में इटली के एक युवा डॉक्टर आंद्रियास वेसेलियस ने [[anatomy|शरीर-रचना]] की एक भारी-भरकम किताब छापी, जिसमें बारीक चित्र थे। ये चित्र उन इंसानी शरीरों पर आधारित थे जिनकी चीर-फाड़ उन्होंने खुद की थी। उन्होंने दिखाया कि गैलेन ने बहुत-सी गलतियाँ की थीं। 1628 में अंग्रेज़ डॉक्टर विलियम हार्वी ने दिखाया कि दिल खून को पूरे शरीर में गोल-गोल एक घेरे में पंप करता है।

1670 के दशक में नीदरलैंड के एक कपड़ा व्यापारी एंटोनी वॉन ल्यूवेनहॉक ने अपने बनाए [[@microscopes|सूक्ष्मदर्शियों]] से पानी में और अपने मुँह में नन्हे [[microorganism|सूक्ष्मजीव]] देखे। 1816 में रेने लेनेक ने लपेटे हुए कागज़ से स्टेथोस्कोप ईजाद किया। 1895 में विल्हेल्म रॉन्टगन ने एक्स-रे खोजीं, और कुछ ही हफ़्तों में डॉक्टर ज़िंदा लोगों के अंदर की हड्डियों की तस्वीरें लेने लगे।

1860 से 1880 के दशकों में फ़्रांस के लुई पाश्चर और जर्मनी के रॉबर्ट कोख ने दिखाया कि बहुत-सी बीमारियाँ [[germ|कीटाणुओं]] से होती हैं। [[@body-handwashing-history|सर्जन हाथ धोने लगे]] और औज़ार साफ़ करने लगे, और ऑपरेशन के बाद कहीं ज़्यादा मरीज़ बचने लगे। [[@vaccines|टीकों]] ने, और बाद में [[@antibiotics|एंटीबायोटिक]] ने, चिकित्सा को फिर से बदल दिया।

मेडिकल कॉलेजों के दरवाज़े धीरे-धीरे खुले। 1849 में एलिज़ाबेथ ब्लैकवेल अमेरिका में मेडिकल डिग्री पाने वाली पहली महिला बनीं। 1886 में महाराष्ट्र की आनंदी गोपाल जोशी ने पेंसिल्वेनिया के एक मेडिकल कॉलेज से पढ़ाई पूरी की। वे पश्चिमी चिकित्सा में प्रशिक्षित पहली भारतीय महिलाओं में से एक थीं। आज दुनिया भर के [[@hospitals|अस्पतालों]] में स्कैनर, [[@future-medicine|जीन की जाँचें]] और नन्हे कैमरे डॉक्टरों को बिना एक भी चीरा लगाए शरीर के अंदर देखने देते हैं।

text: अंगदान का मतलब है अपने शरीर का कोई हिस्सा किसी ऐसे इंसान की मदद के लिए देना जिसका अपना [[organ|अंग]] ठीक से काम करना बंद कर चुका हो। अंग को एक ऑपरेशन से दूसरे शरीर में लगाया जाता है, जिसे प्रत्यारोपण या ट्रांसप्लांट कहते हैं। गुर्दे, लिवर, दिल, फेफड़े और पैंक्रियास, सबका प्रत्यारोपण हो सकता है, और कुछ [[tissue|ऊतकों]] का भी, जैसे आँख का [[cornea|कॉर्निया]], त्वचा और दिल के वाल्व।

ज़्यादातर अंग उन लोगों से आते हैं जिनकी अस्पताल में मौत हुई हो, अक्सर दिमाग पर गंभीर चोट के बाद, और जिनके परिवार दान के लिए राज़ी हों। कुछ अंग जीवित दानदाताओं से आते हैं, जो अपने दो [[@kidneys|गुर्दों]] में से एक या लिवर का एक हिस्सा देते हैं। मौत के बाद एक दानदाता आठ लोगों तक की मदद कर सकता है, और दान किए गए ऊतकों से कई और की।

लंबे समय तक प्रत्यारोपण नाकाम होते रहे। मरीज़ का [[@immune-system|रोग-प्रतिरोधक तंत्र]], जो शरीर को कीटाणुओं से बचाता है, नए अंग पर ऐसे हमला कर देता था जैसे वह कोई घुसपैठिया हो।

1954 में बोस्टन के एक अस्पताल में सर्जन जोसेफ़ मरे ने रोनाल्ड हेरिक का एक गुर्दा उनके हूबहू जुड़वाँ भाई रिचर्ड में लगाया। जुड़वाँ भाइयों के [[gene|जीन]] लगभग एक जैसे होते हैं, इसलिए रिचर्ड के शरीर ने गुर्दा अपना लिया। बाद में मरे को नोबेल पुरस्कार मिला। 1960 और 1970 के दशक तक रोग-प्रतिरोधक तंत्र को शांत करने वाली नई दवाइयों से ऐसे लोगों के बीच भी अंग लगाना मुमकिन हो गया जो जुड़वाँ नहीं थे।

sec.h: जब दानदाता की मौत हो चुकी हो

sec.t:
तुम्हारे दो गुर्दे हैं, पर एक के साथ भी सेहतमंद ज़िंदगी जी सकते हो। इसलिए माता-पिता, भाई, बहन या पति-पत्नी परिवार के किसी सदस्य को एक गुर्दा दे सकते हैं। [[@liver|लिवर]] तो और भी अनोखा है। सर्जन किसी जीवित दानदाता के लिवर का एक हिस्सा निकाल सकते हैं, और दोनों टुकड़े कुछ महीनों में बढ़कर लगभग पूरे आकार के हो जाते हैं।

जीवित दानदाताओं की पहले कई जाँचें होती हैं, ताकि पक्का हो सके कि दान करना उनके लिए सुरक्षित है। भारत में ज़्यादातर प्रत्यारोपण जीवित दानदाताओं से होते हैं, अक्सर माँएँ और पत्नियाँ परिवार के सदस्यों को अंग देती हैं।

भारत में 2024 में लगभग 18,900 प्रत्यारोपण हुए, जो एक रिकॉर्ड है। पर मौत के बाद अंगदान अब भी बहुत कम है, हर दस लाख लोगों पर एक से भी कम दानदाता। तमिलनाडु, तेलंगाना, कर्नाटक, महाराष्ट्र और गुजरात में इसके मज़बूत कार्यक्रम हैं। 1994 में बने भारत के प्रत्यारोपण क़ानून ने ब्रेन डेथ के नियम तय किए और अंगों की ख़रीद-बिक्री पर रोक लगाई।

अमेरिका में 1,00,000 से ज़्यादा लोग इंतज़ार की सूची में हैं। बहुत-से अमेरिकी ड्राइविंग लाइसेंस बनवाते समय दानदाता के तौर पर नाम लिखवाते हैं। भारत में बड़े लोग सरकार की नोटो (NOTTO) वेबसाइट पर ऑनलाइन अंगदान का संकल्प ले सकते हैं।

अंगदान मुश्किल विषय लग सकता है, क्योंकि इसमें बीमारी और मौत की बात आती है। डॉक्टर और अंगदान से जुड़े समूह कहते हैं कि परिवार जो सबसे काम की चीज़ कर सकते हैं, वह है पहले से शांति से इस पर बात करना, ताकि सब एक-दूसरे की इच्छा जानते हों।

बच्चे ख़ुद दानदाता के रूप में नाम नहीं लिखवा सकते, पर वे सीख सकते हैं कि शरीर कैसे काम करता है, और सवाल पूछ सकते हैं। अगर तुम और जानना चाहते हो, तो माता-पिता, टीचर या डॉक्टर से बात करना अच्छा रहेगा। लगाया गया हर दिल, हर गुर्दा और हर कॉर्निया किसी के देने के फ़ैसले से शुरू हुआ।

text: पूरे शरीर में नसों के कुछ खास सिरे फैले हैं जो नुकसान को भाँपते हैं। वैज्ञानिक इन्हें नोसिसेप्टर कहते हैं, लैटिन के एक शब्द से जिसका मतलब है चोट या हानि। कुछ तेज़ दबाव पर जागते हैं, कुछ बहुत ज़्यादा गर्मी या ठंड पर, और कुछ चोटिल [[cell|कोशिकाओं]] से निकलने वाले रसायनों पर।

जब ये जागते हैं, तो [[nerve|नसों]] के रास्ते मेरुरज्जु तक और फिर दिमाग तक संकेत भेजते हैं। फिर दिमाग तय करता है कि क्या हो रहा है, और दर्द का एहसास पैदा करता है। इसे जान-बूझकर बुरा लगने वाला बनाया गया है, क्योंकि दर्द का काम है तुम्हें रोकना और चोट वाले हिस्से को बचाना। टकराया अँगूठा तुम्हें उछलने और उसे पकड़ने पर मजबूर करता है। दुखता टखना तुम्हें लँगड़ाकर चलवाता है, ताकि उसे भरने का समय मिले।

sec.t:
अँगूठा टकराए, तो शायद तुम्हें दो दर्द महसूस हों। पहले एक तेज़, तीखी चुभन आती है। एक पल बाद हल्का, धड़कता हुआ दर्द आता है। ये अलग-अलग तरह के नस-रेशों से चलते हैं। तेज़ वाले चिकनाई की एक परत में लिपटे होते हैं जो संकेत को तेज़ी से दौड़ाती है। धीमे वालों पर यह परत नहीं होती।

तीखा दर्द ठीक-ठीक बताता है कि कहाँ और क्या हुआ। धीमा दर्द तुम्हें बार-बार याद दिलाता रहता है कि चोट का ख़याल रखो। दर्द पहुँचने से पहले ही कोई [[@reflexes|रिफ़्लेक्स]] शायद तुम्हारा पैर झटके से हटा चुका होता है।

बहुत ही कम लोग ऐसे पैदा होते हैं जिन्हें दर्द महसूस ही नहीं होता। सुनने में यह वरदान लगता है, पर यह ख़तरनाक है। इस हालत वाले बच्चे बिना पता चले हड्डियाँ तोड़ सकते हैं, जीभ काट सकते हैं या ख़ुद को जला सकते हैं। उन्हें हर रोज़ अपने शरीर को सावधानी से जाँचना सीखना पड़ता है।

इससे पता चलता है कि दर्द क्यों ज़रूरी है। यह शरीर का अलार्म है। 2021 में अमेरिकी वैज्ञानिक डेविड जूलियस को गर्मी भाँपने वाला सेंसर खोजने के लिए नोबेल पुरस्कार में हिस्सा मिला। उन्होंने इसे [[capsaicin|कैप्सेसिन]] पर खोजबीन करके ढूँढा, जो वह रसायन है जिससे [[@chillies|मिर्च]] जलती है। यह ठीक वही सेंसर जगा देता है जो असली गर्मी जगाती है। इसीलिए [[@spicy-hot|तीखा खाना गर्म लगता है]], भले वह ठंडा हो।

इंसान हमेशा से [[@oddity-old-medicine|दर्द कम करने के तरीके ढूँढते]] आए हैं। प्राचीन मिस्र और यूनान के लोग विलो की छाल चबाते थे। 1800 के दशक में रसायनशास्त्रियों ने उसका असरदार पदार्थ ढूँढा, और 1899 में बायर कंपनी ने उसका एक रूप एस्पिरिन के नाम से बेचना शुरू किया।

पहले सर्जरी मरीज़ों के पूरी तरह जागते हुए होती थी। प्राचीन भारत में [[@sushruta|सुश्रुत]] संहिता में ऑपरेशन से पहले मरीज़ों को मदिरा देने का ज़िक्र है। 1846 में बोस्टन में विलियम मॉर्टन नाम के एक दाँतों के डॉक्टर ने सबके सामने दिखाया कि ईथर सुँघाने से ऑपरेशन के दौरान मरीज़ सो सकता है। आज [[anaesthesia|बेहोशी की दवाइयाँ]] और दर्द की दवाइयाँ सर्जरी को सुरक्षित और बिना दर्द का बनाती हैं। लंबे समय तक रहने वाले दर्द का इलाज अब भी मुश्किल है, इसलिए अगर कोई चीज़ बहुत दिनों तक दुखे, तो किसी बड़े या डॉक्टर को बताना ज़रूरी है।

text: A data centre is a building packed with computers called [[server|servers]]. They are stacked in tall metal cabinets called racks, row after row, often in halls as big as a football field. Each server stores files or runs programs for people far away.

When you watch a video, send a message or ask a map app for directions, your phone talks to servers in a data centre. These buildings need three things above all: a steady supply of electricity, fast connections to the internet, and a way to get rid of the heat. Everything else is designed around those needs.

sec.t:
Walk into a data hall and the first thing you notice is the noise: a loud, steady roar from thousands of fans. Each rack holds dozens of flat servers slotted in like books on a shelf. Bundles of cables run overhead or under a raised floor, carrying power and data.

Some servers do the thinking, with powerful chips. Others are mostly storage, crammed with hard drives or memory chips. Fibre-optic cables connect the building to the wider [[@internet-how|internet]], often through several different routes, so one cut cable doesn't knock everything offline. Security is tight. Many sites have fences, guards and fingerprint or card scanners at every door.

Almost every bit of electricity a server uses turns into heat. Packed together, servers would quickly overheat and break. So a large part of a data centre is really a giant cooling machine.

The usual trick is to arrange racks in "hot aisles" and "cold aisles". Cool air is blown in at the front of the servers and hot air leaves at the back, where it is pulled away. Big chillers work like an [[@air-conditioning|air conditioner]] the size of a house. Newer chips for artificial intelligence run so hot that some are cooled with liquid flowing through pipes right next to them.

{{story:air-conditioning}}

Location helps. Google's data centre at Hamina in Finland uses cold seawater from the Baltic. In hot places such as Chennai or Arizona, cooling costs more.

A data centre is expected to keep running even during [[@what-if-no-electricity|a power cut]]. Rooms full of [[@batteries|batteries]] take over instantly if the mains supply fails. Within seconds, diesel generators the size of a shipping container start up and keep the lights on for hours or days.

The biggest companies copy your data to several buildings, sometimes in different countries. If a flood or fire hits one, another takes over. That is why your photos don't vanish when one machine dies.

sec.h: Where they are, and the cost
sec.t:
Northern Virginia, near Washington DC, has more data centres than anywhere else on Earth, partly because some of the early internet's main connections met there. In India, Mumbai and Navi Mumbai host the largest share, helped by the [[@undersea-internet|undersea cables]] that land on the coast nearby. Chennai, Hyderabad and Delhi's surrounding region are growing fast.

All this uses a lot of power. The International Energy Agency estimates data centres used about 1.5% of the world's electricity in 2024, and expects that to rise quickly as artificial intelligence spreads. If that electricity comes from coal, it adds to [[@climate-change|climate change]]. So companies are signing deals for solar and wind power and trying to use less water for cooling. In parts of Scandinavia, the waste heat from servers is piped into homes to keep them warm in winter.

text: चाणक्य एक ब्राह्मण विद्वान थे, जो परंपरा के अनुसार लगभग 300 ईसा पूर्व में हुए। कहा जाता है कि वे तक्षशिला में पढ़ाते थे, जो शिक्षा का एक मशहूर केंद्र था और आज पाकिस्तान में है।

सबसे जानी-मानी कहानी यह है कि मगध के नंद राजा के दरबार में उनका अपमान हुआ, और उन्होंने इस [[dynasty|राजवंश]] को मिटाने की क़सम खाई। उन्हें चंद्रगुप्त नाम का एक होनहार नौजवान मिला। चाणक्य ने उसे तैयार किया और गद्दी तक पहुँचाया। यहीं से [[@mauryan-empire|मौर्य साम्राज्य]] की शुरुआत हुई। चाणक्य को कौटिल्य भी कहते हैं। यही नाम राज चलाने पर लिखी संस्कृत की एक मशहूर किताब *अर्थशास्त्र* पर दर्ज है।

sec.h: एक किताब, जो खोई और फिर मिली
sec.t:
सदियों तक लोग अर्थशास्त्र को बस दूसरी किताबों में आए ज़िक्र से जानते थे। फिर 1905 में ताड़ के पत्तों पर लिखी [[manuscript|पांडुलिपियों]] का एक गट्ठर मैसूर की ओरिएंटल लाइब्रेरी को सौंपा गया। वहाँ के पुस्तकालय-अध्यक्ष आर. शामशास्त्री समझ गए कि उनके हाथ में वही खोई हुई किताब है।

उन्होंने इसे 1909 में संस्कृत में और 1915 में अंग्रेज़ी में छापा। दुनिया भर के विद्वान हैरान रह गए। प्राचीन भारत से शासन की एक पूरी, बारीक गाइड सामने थी, जिसमें ऐसे विषय थे जिनकी चिंता लोग सिर्फ़ आज की सरकारों की मानते थे। इस खोज ने इतिहासकारों की नज़र बदल दी। पता चला कि यहाँ के विचारकों ने धर्म और कविता के साथ-साथ पैसे, क़ानून और सत्ता पर भी गहराई से लिखा था।

लेखक अक्सर कौटिल्य की तुलना इटली के निकोलो मैकियावेली से करते हैं, जिसने 1513 में *द प्रिंस* लिखी थी। वह भी शासकों के लिए एक दो-टूक गाइड है। दोनों सत्ता को वैसा दिखाते हैं जैसी वह असल में चलती है, वैसा नहीं जैसा लोग चाहते हैं।

पर अर्थशास्त्र यह भी कहता है कि राजा का सुख उसकी प्रजा के सुख में है। इसमें ठीक मज़दूरी के नियम हैं, बेईमान अफ़सरों के लिए सज़ा है, और अनाथों व बुज़ुर्गों की मदद की बात है। इसलिए पढ़ने वालों को इसमें ठंडी रणनीति भी मिलती है और अच्छे शासन की सच्ची फ़िक्र भी।

उनके अपने समय का कोई [[inscription|शिलालेख]] उनका नाम नहीं लेता। उनकी ज़िंदगी की कहानियाँ बौद्ध, जैन और हिंदू ग्रंथों से आती हैं, जो बहुत बाद में लिखे गए, और ब्योरों पर ये आपस में मेल नहीं खाते। संस्कृत का एक मशहूर नाटक *मुद्राराक्षस* उन्हें एक विरोधी मंत्री को मात देते दिखाता है, पर यह भी उनके कई सदियों बाद लिखा गया।

कुछ विद्वान सोचते हैं कि समय के साथ चाणक्य और कौटिल्य दो अलग लोग होकर भी एक ही किरदार में घुल-मिल गए होंगे। किताब ख़ुद पुराने गुरुओं का ज़िक्र करती है और लगता है कि यह धीरे-धीरे, कई चरणों में बढ़ी। यानी यह इंसान कुछ इतिहास है और कुछ किंवदंती।

भारत में उनका नाम हर जगह है। छोटी-छोटी सूक्तियों का एक संग्रह *चाणक्य नीति* घरों और दफ़्तरों में ख़ूब दोहराया जाता है, हालाँकि इसे उनके बहुत बाद जोड़ा गया। [[@delhi|दिल्ली]] में जिस इलाक़े में कई देशों के दूतावास हैं, उसका नाम चाणक्यपुरी है। राजनयिकों से भरी जगह के लिए इससे सटीक नाम क्या होता।

टीवी धारावाहिकों और फ़िल्मों ने उन्हें चतुर रणनीति का नायक बना दिया है। दुनिया भर में राजनीति पढ़ने वाले आज भी अर्थशास्त्र को राजकाज की सबसे पुरानी गाइडों में से एक मानकर पढ़ते हैं।

text: Polynesian sailors found their way across the Pacific by reading nature. They steered by the rising and setting points of stars and felt the long ocean swells rolling under their canoes. They watched which way birds flew at dusk, and noticed clouds piling up over hidden islands.

They sailed in big double-hulled canoes, two hulls joined by a deck, with sails woven from pandanus leaves. These canoes could carry families, pigs, chickens, dogs and plants to start a new life. Food for the voyage included breadfruit, taro, coconuts and dried fish.

Over about 2,000 years, they spread across a huge triangle of ocean, from [[@hawaii-culture|Hawaiʻi]] in the north to [[@new-zealand|Aotearoa New Zealand]] in the south-west and Rapa Nui in the east. They reached almost every island where people could live.

st.prompt: Far out at sea, a Polynesian navigator spots a seabird called a tern flying home at dusk. What does that tell them?

options.t: Land is probably within a day's sail in that direction
A storm is coming in the next hour
The canoe is near the equator

st.reveal: Some seabirds fly out to fish in the morning and return to land at dusk, usually staying within about 30 to 50 km of home. Following them at sunset can point the way to an island.

d.try: On a clear night, with an adult, pick one bright star low on the eastern horizon and note what's under it, like a tree or a roof. Check again an hour later. The star will have risen and moved west. Polynesian navigators memorised where hundreds of stars rose and set, and used them like a compass.
myth: The Pacific islands were settled by accident, by people blown off course on drifting canoes.

Computer studies of winds and currents show drifting canoes would almost never reach distant islands like Hawaiʻi. Voyages like Hōkūleʻa's showed that Polynesians could sail there and back on purpose, using stars, waves and birds.

from islands near New Guinea, about 3,000 years ago

sec.t:
The voyagers' ancestors came originally from Taiwan and the islands of South-East Asia. By about 3,000 years ago, a people known to [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] by their pottery, called Lapita, were sailing east from islands near New Guinea to Fiji, Tonga and Samoa.

There they stayed for centuries, and Polynesian culture took shape. Then, around 1,000 years ago, a burst of long voyages carried people to the far corners of the triangle: Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and finally Aotearoa, settled around 1250 to 1300 CE.

sec.h: A star compass in the head
sec.t:
Navigators trained from childhood. They memorised where dozens of [[@constellations|stars]] rose and set on the horizon. Each star's rising point was like a house on a giant circle, a "star compass" kept in memory.

As one star climbed too high to use, the navigator switched to the next one rising at the same spot. By day, they steered by the Sun and by the swells. A swell is a long wave made by a far-off storm, which can keep a steady direction for days. Some navigators lay down in the hull to feel the [[@waves-how|waves]] crossing beneath them.

Signs of land helped close the gap. Clouds often pile up over islands, and [[lagoon|lagoons]] can tint their undersides green. Floating plants, and seabirds heading home at sunset, also showed the way.

{{story:constellations}}

By the 20th century, many outsiders doubted Polynesians had sailed on purpose. Some thought they had simply drifted. In 1947, the Norwegian explorer Thor Heyerdahl even argued they had come from South America, and drifted west on a raft called the *Kon-Tiki* to show it was possible.

In 1976, a group in Hawaiʻi built a replica double canoe called *Hōkūleʻa*. No Hawaiian navigator still knew the old methods, so they asked Mau Piailug, from the tiny Micronesian island of Satawal. Using no instruments, he guided the canoe about 4,000 km to Tahiti in about a month. Huge crowds met them on the beach.

Mau went on to teach Hawaiian navigators, and from 2014 to 2017 *Hōkūleʻa* sailed right around the world.

Polynesians grew the sweet potato, a plant from South America, long before Europeans arrived. And a DNA study published in 2020 suggested that some Polynesians and Native South Americans met around 800 years ago.

Who travelled to whom is still debated. Many experts think Polynesian sailors reached South America and came back, but the evidence isn't settled.

Across the Pacific, people are reviving traditional voyaging. Young navigators in Hawaiʻi, Aotearoa and Micronesia learn the star compass and sail long trips. The skills that once filled an ocean with people have become a source of pride. They are also a reminder that careful watching can [[@migration|find the way]] across a sea with no roads at all.

text: Los Angeles, often called LA, is the second-biggest city in the USA and the home of Hollywood, the American film industry. It is known for sunshine, beaches, long freeways and a skyline backed by mountains. Nearly 10 million people live in Los Angeles County (2024 estimate).

LA is also one of the most mixed cities in the world. People with roots in Mexico, [[@seoul|Korea]], the Philippines, China, Armenia, Iran, India and many other places live there, and more than 200 languages are spoken. It has hosted the Olympics twice and is due to host them again in 2028.

st.reveal: The sign said HOLLYWOODLAND and was put up to sell homes in the hills. It was meant to last only about a year and a half. In 1949 the last four letters were taken down, and it became a symbol of the film industry.

sec.h: A small village by a river
sec.t:
Long before the city, the Tongva people lived in villages across the basin. In 1781, a group of 44 settlers came from New Spain, now Mexico, and founded a farming village near the Los Angeles River. They were of mixed Spanish, Indigenous and African roots. The village was named El Pueblo de la Reina de los Ángeles, the Town of the Queen of the Angels.

LA was part of Mexico until 1848, when it passed to the United States after a war. Railways, oranges and then oil helped it grow from a small town into a giant city in less than a century.

In the early 1900s, film companies started moving to Los Angeles from the east coast. The sun shone most of the year, which mattered when films needed natural light. Within a few hours' drive were beaches, deserts, mountains and forests, so one place could stand in for anywhere. Land was cheap, too.

By the 1920s, [[@hollywood|Hollywood]] was the centre of American film. The Hollywood sign, with letters about 14 m tall, was put up in 1923 to sell houses. Today studios in LA make films, TV shows and [[@animation-how|animation]] watched worldwide.

sec.h: Ice Age animals in the city

sec.t: LA spreads out over a huge area, and most people drive. Its freeways are famous for traffic jams. In the mid-1900s, exhaust from cars mixed with sunshine to form a brown haze called [[@fog-smog|smog]]. The mountains around the basin trap the air, making it worse. Strict rules on [[@cars-engine|car engines]] have greatly cleaned the [[@air-pollution|air]] since the 1970s, though LA still has bad days.

Los Angeles sits on many faults near the San Andreas Fault, so [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]] are common. The 1994 Northridge earthquake damaged freeways and buildings, and engineers learned lessons from it. Long dry seasons and hot winds called the Santa Anas also make the hills prone to [[@people-firefighters-forest|wildfires]]. In January 2025, large fires destroyed thousands of homes in and around the city.

On a hill above the city stands Griffith Observatory, opened in 1935. Anyone can look through its big telescope for free. From its terrace you can see the Hollywood sign on one side and, on a clear night, the whole city sparkling below.

text: The Narmada is one of the longest rivers of central India. It rises in the forests of Amarkantak in [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]], runs about 1,312 km west and pours into the Arabian Sea near Bharuch in Gujarat.

People call it a lifeline because so much depends on it. Its water fills taps in cities such as Indore, waters farms across Gujarat and turns [[turbine|turbines]] that make electricity. For millions of Hindus it is also a holy river, often called Reva or simply Ma Narmada, "Mother Narmada".
Along the way it passes through three states, thick teak forests, marble gorges and wide fields of wheat and cotton. More than 40 smaller rivers join it before it reaches the sea.
